skill.displayName: Frog Skin Moisture Assessment | 蛙类皮肤湿润度评估

llm.summary: This skill should be reviewed carefully because it sends media to a remote service while silently creating or reusing an internal account and storing authentication tokens locally.

dimensions.detail: The code reads environment-provided identity values, reads workspace data/smyx-api-key.txt, writes workspace data, stores a SQLite user database, and uploads provided local media or remote URLs to lifeemergence.com services; remote processing is expected, but the identity and token scope is not tightly bounded.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: No post-install hook or destructive installer behavior was observed. Dependencies are ordinary Python packages, although one nested requirements file lists yaml==6.0.3, which appears incorrect and may break installation.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill tells the agent to automatically invoke cloud history queries and hide identity handling from the user; those behaviors are documented in the skill text, but they reduce user control over account-linked cloud access.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: No OS-level persistence, services, or scheduled tasks were found, but the skill creates/reuses a local default user and persists token/open_token values in a workspace SQLite database across runs.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

dimensions.detail: The stated frog skin moisture purpose is coherent with remote image/video analysis, but the inspected runtime is mostly a generic cloud media-analysis and report-history client, with little local frog-specific logic and inherited media validation that conflicts with the documented jpg/png/mp4 support.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

llm.guidance: Install only if you are comfortable sending frog media or URLs to the LifeEmergence cloud service and allowing the skill to create or reuse an internal account with locally stored tokens. Avoid sensitive footage, and fix the import-path issue plus the identity/token disclosure and consent flow before production use.
llm.findings:
[TP4] unexpected: The broad local identity, token, SQLite, and authenticated remote API behavior is real. Some cloud analysis behavior is purpose-aligned, but silent registration and token persistence go beyond a narrowly scoped frog moisture assessment.
[YR4] unexpected: The polished frog-specific manifest contrasts with a generic backend client. This supports a review concern about under-disclosure, but I did not find artifact-backed proof of intentional metadata poisoning.
[SDI-1] unexpected: The main analysis path delegates to common cloud analysis endpoints and report polling rather than implementing local frog skin gloss or moisture analysis; this may work if the backend enforces the scene code, but the package itself is broader and more generic than the description implies.
[SDI-2] unexpected: The user/account model includes personal and token fields and is used to cache backend authentication, which is only partly disclosed and not necessary for pure media analysis.
[LP3] unexpected: The artifact has no clear least-privilege permission boundary while using filesystem, environment, network, local database, and output-file writes.
[SQP-1] unexpected: Automatic triggers for media analysis and history listing are broad enough to cause cloud upload or account-linked history access with little explicit confirmation.
[SQP-3] expected: The Chinese-first behavior is visible throughout the skill text and appears to be a locale/product issue rather than hidden security behavior.
[P9] expected: The whitespace finding corresponds to Python line wrapping/alignment in inspected code; I did not find hidden instructions in that area.
[T07] unexpected: The sys.path insertion before absolute imports is a real local module-hijacking vulnerability. I treat it as an unsafe coding issue, not as evidence of malicious intent.
